slides.notes:
SAY: A function is a named piece of code that a program can run whenever it needs that work done, from as many places as it likes. The textbook describes it as a mini program within a program (Sweigart, 2025), and the Python glossary states the same idea more formally: a series of statements which returns some value to a caller, and which can also be passed zero or more arguments that are used while its body runs (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - Function.
slides.take: If you can answer these, chapter 4 is yours

slides.title: Frames and scope
slides.sub: Where calls live, and which x you mean
slides.notes:
SAY: A frame is the record that Python keeps for one running function call, and the call stack is the pile of such records that exist at a given moment. The language reference explains that a code block is executed in an execution frame, which contains some administrative information and determines where and how execution continues after the block's execution has completed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - Frames.

slides.title: 1952: the function gets invented

items.cap: EDSAC - Computer Laboratory, University of Cambridge, CC BY 2.0

items: EDSAC, Cambridge: one of the first stored-program machines
Wheeler's problem: jump into shared code AND find the way back
His closed subroutine is the ancestor of every def here
The call stack is his return-address bookkeeping, grown up

items.who: David Wheeler, on EDSAC at the University of Cambridge
items.where: the Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory; published through the ACM

slides.notes:
STORY (1952): On EDSAC, one of the first stored-program computers, David Wheeler worked out how a program could jump into a reusable block of code and - the hard part - find its way back to wherever it came from. His 'closed subroutine' and the jump-and-return it needed (long called the Wheeler jump) are the ancestor of every def on these slides, and the call stack the chapter draws is the modern descendant of his return-address bookkeeping.
SOURCE: David Wheeler's closed-subroutine work on EDSAC, Cambridge, published 1952 through the ACM ('The use of sub-routines in programmes'); the return linkage is historically known as the Wheeler jump. Photo: EDSAC, Computer Laboratory, University of Cambridge, CC BY 2.0.
slides.take: def and return are 1952 inventions you use every day

slides.title: Errors, handled
slides.sub: try, except - and where to put them
slides.notes:
SAY: Error handling is the part of a program that decides what happens when something goes wrong. In Python an error that stops a statement is called an exception, and the language has two statements for dealing with it: try marks the code that might fail, and except says what to do when it does.

slides.title: The except clause sheds its parentheses
slides.sub: Python 3.14, 2025

items: For decades: except (ValueError, TypeError) - parentheses required
PEP 758, shipped in 3.14: the bare pair now parses - and this build RAN it

items.cap: program except758_v1_0_0.py, lines 1 to 4 of 4, run under Python 3.14.6
items.label: executed under the build's 3.14.6; on 3.13 this file is a SyntaxError

items.who: proposed and accepted through the CPython core developers' PEP process

slides.notes:
STORY (Python 3.14, 2025): For decades, catching two exception types required parentheses: except (ValueError, TypeError). PEP 758 let the parentheses go, and Python 3.14 ships it. This deck does not take the release notes' word for it: the chapter program with the bare except clause was EXECUTED under Python 3.14 during this build, and its transcript on the slide is what that interpreter printed. On 3.13 the same file is a SyntaxError - version truth, demonstrated.
SOURCE: PEP 758 ('Allow except and except* expressions without parentheses'), accepted for Python 3.14 (peps.python.org/pep-0758); the chapter program except758_v1_0_0.py runs clean under the build's 3.14.6 and raises SyntaxError under 3.13 - both observed during this build.
slides.take: Language change is checkable - this slide ran on 3.14

slides.title: The unsolved problem in your homework
slides.sub: posed 1937; still open

items: Halve if even, triple-and-add-one if odd: Collatz (1937) says you always reach 1 - unproven since; Erdos offered 500 dollars

items.cap: program collatz_v1_0_0.py, lines 1 to 12 of 12, run under Python 3.14.6
items.label: the rule as a function, fed 3 - eight steps to 1

items.who: Lothar Collatz; famously weighed by Paul Erdos
items.where: Hamburg; the chapter's own collatz program

slides.notes:
STORY (posed 1937; still open): Take any positive integer: halve it if even, triple-and-add-one if odd, repeat. Lothar Collatz conjectured in 1937 that you always reach 1. Nobody has proved it; Paul Erdos said mathematics is not yet ripe for such questions and offered 500 dollars for a proof. The chapter's collatz program is this exact rule as a function - your homework walks a problem that has outlasted every mathematician since.
SOURCE: The Collatz conjecture, posed 1937, open to this day; Erdos's remark and 500-dollar offer are standard in its literature - summarized with references at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collatz_conjecture. The chapter program collatz_v1_0_0.py implements the rule.
slides.take: A five-line function can hold an unsolved problem
